title: When Your Pricing Faces Pushback, Negotiate Before You Lose the Deal
documentTitle: Epic Games, Inc. v. Apple Inc. — Exhibit A: App Store Membership Subscriptions Update
excerptForBlog: Phil and Eddy, To follow up on our discussion on Friday, attached is an updated overview of App Store Membership Subscriptions for developers who offer physical goods and services. As I mentioned, the team has spoken to several developers and they've consistently pushed back on the 30% commission, so we may need your help to come up with some creative solutions to make this happen. Please let us know if you need more information or have any questions for your discussion.

lessonTitle: When Your Pricing Faces Pushback, Negotiate Before You Lose the Deal
pullQuote: The moment your partners consistently refuse your terms, you have two choices: lose them or adapt — and waiting too long to decide is its own decision.
leadershipTraits: escalates with evidence, not just problems
reads market signals before they become crises
protects the headline rate while seeking flexibility at the edges
keeps senior stakeholders in the loop with minimal friction
situation: On August 21, 2018, Matt Fischer — context suggests he led App Store business at Apple — sent a brief internal note to Phil and Eddy following a Friday discussion. The memo flags that developers who sell physical goods and services through the App Store were consistently pushing back on Apple's 30% commission. Fischer is escalating the problem upward and asking senior leadership to help find, in his words, 'creative solutions.'
insight:
The phrase 'consistently pushed back' is the key signal here. Fischer isn't reporting one unhappy developer — he's reporting a pattern. When multiple independent customers raise the same objection, that's pricing pressure made visible. It often means the price-to-value ratio has drifted out of alignment for a specific segment.

What Fischer is actually doing is classic **segment differentiation**: recognizing that a single commission rate may not fit every use case equally. Developers selling physical goods don't receive the same distribution, payment, or fraud-protection value from the App Store as, say, a game developer does. The 30% that works in one context can feel extractive in another. Escalating to senior leadership rather than defending the current rate suggests the team read the signal seriously and understood it required a structural response, not just a sales objection to overcome.
application: If you run a platform or service with a standard pricing tier, build a regular feedback loop with your highest-friction customers — the ones most likely to churn or complain. When you hear the same objection from several independent sources, don't dismiss it. Map whether the objection clusters around a specific use case or segment. That cluster is your signal to consider a separate tier, adjusted terms, or a different value proposition — before the friction turns into defection.
